problems.description: 13 measured convention violations across the new/changed files: classes not PascalCase, module constants not UPPER_CASE, and non-snake_case functions in app.py, celery_config.py, and conftest.py — convention score 0.64, a clear adherence regression.

Session 1 discards the seed's modular Blueprint structure and SQLite persistence entirely (-247 lines net), replacing it with a single flat-file JSON store guarded by an in-process threading.Lock — no cross-process concurrency safety, transactions, or durability guarantees, so the new code regresses the existing persistence pattern.
celery_config.py introduces a Celery task-queue dependency that is architecturally mismatched with the flat-file, in-process-Lock store; heavyweight worker machinery for a simple JSON-backed API.
The -247/+158 line shift collapses a modular multi-file app into a smaller surface, reducing separation of concerns compared to the Blueprints layout the seed established.

strengths: All SonarQube deltas are non-negative: -4 smells, -1 cognitive complexity, +0 bugs, +0.0% duplications — the replacement is measurably simpler code than the seed.
Retains the Flask framework from the seed (stack continuity) and writes a clear, scoped docstring.
New code uses timezone-aware datetimes (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) and pathlib, and acknowledges concurrency with a threading.Lock around the store.
commit_reviews.summary: The greenfield replacement is measurably simpler and cleaner code (no new bugs, fewer smells), but it tears down the seed's modular/SQLite architecture, adds a mismatched Celery config, and lands a 0.64 convention score with 13 naming violations, making this a net architectural and conventions regression.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (manual HMAC-SHA256/base64url encode/decode) instead of a maintained library like PyJWT or flask-jwt-extended. Lacks iat/nbf/aud/iss claims and relies on app-internal encoding logic that can drift from spec.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded predictable value ('development-secret-change-me') when the env var is unset, enabling token forgery in any deployment that forgets to set it.
No token revocation/logout mechanism; _current_user_from_token re-reads the entire flat-file store on every request, compounding the existing O(n) read/write-per-request pattern as users grow.
Manual _encode_part/_decode_part base64 padding handling plus hand-rolled token lifecycle is subtle code that a library would eliminate; adds +22 cognitive complexity and +2 smells per SonarQube.
Migration silently orphan-izes pre-auth tasks (owner_id=None tasks are invisible to all users), and init_db backfills next_user_id but not owner_id ownership of existing tasks.

Mechanical convention score is 0.64 with 13 violations, but the listed violations are in celery_config.py and conftest.py (untouched by this diff) — this commit itself introduces no new classes or module-level constants; score likely reflects pre-existing repo state, not this change.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash and signatures compared in constant time via hmac.compare_digest
Ownership scoping consistently enforced across create, list, get, and update routes via owner_id filtering
Graceful backward-compatible migration for pre-auth stores (setdefault owner_id=None, next_user_id backfill)
Reuses the established flat-file store + _storage_lock + jsonify patterns rather than introducing new infrastructure
Clean 401/400/409 error semantics and use of flask.g for request-scoped current user
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-scoped auth feature that fits the flat-file app's existing patterns with solid password hashing and per-user task isolation, but the hand-rolled JWT with a predictable fallback secret adds security and maintainability debt.

problems.description: Adds a Celery + Redis broker (celery_config.py, notifications.py) to deliver a mocked email that only writes a log line — heavyweight async machinery that introduces a broker dependency, a worker process, and new operational surface to a simple Flask+JSON-store app; a synchronous/logging call or a lighter threading approach would fit the existing architecture.

The notification dispatch block is dedented to function scope (outside the task-update loop) while referencing loop-scoped state ('became_completed', 'owner'), producing tangled cross-scope coupling — consistent with the +9 cognitive complexity delta. Fragile to future multi-task or early-return edits, and relies on the early _not_found() return to avoid NameErrors.

Broad `except Exception:` around send_notification_email.delay swallows all failure modes; the comment documents intent, but it will also mask real bugs (e.g., a bad task signature) as silent log lines.

Recipient fallback `(owner or {}).get('email') or (owner or {}).get('username')` sends notifications to a bare username when no email exists — not a deliverable address, so the fallback silently changes recipient semantics.

Convention score 0.64 flags lowercase module-level names (app, celery_app, broker_url, result_backend). These are framework-idiomatic Flask/Celery patterns, so most flagged violations are false positives; the real delta is the added cognitive complexity, not naming.

strengths: Clean module separation: Celery config (celery_config.py) and the task (notifications.py) are isolated from app.py rather than inlined.
Tests stub .delay via monkeypatch/Mock — deterministic, no broker required, and they verify both the happy path and the transition-only behavior.
Completion transition logic is correct: was_completed → became_completed ensures the notification fires only on the actual completed transition, not on later re-updates.
Broker outage is handled gracefully so a notification failure never turns a successful task update into an error response.
Email is validated as a non-empty string and persisted at registration, following the existing input-validation and store-mutation patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-tested completion-notification feature with correct transition semantics and clean module separation, but the heavyweight Celery+Redis dependency and the awkwardly-scoped dispatch block (+9 cognitive complexity, function-level state coupling) add net technical debt that outweighs the feature for a logging-only email.

problems.description: Measured convention score is 0.64 with 13 violations; app.py reports classes not using PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, which conflicts with the clean PascalCase names (TaskRepository, UserRepository) visible in the diff — flagging the discrepancy between qualitative read and measurement.

_task_repository()/_user_repository() instantiate a fresh repository object on every request; harmless given the shared lock and file-path construction, but a module-level singleton or factory cache would avoid repeated allocation.
Repositories receive _storage_lock as a constructor argument, coupling the data-access layer to Flask's threading lock mechanism; a lock-owned-by-repository or lock-injection seam would be cleaner.
Cognitive complexity +4 per SonarQube delta despite the deduplication; likely concentrated in the new repository methods, so the net complexity move should be verified.

strengths: Extracts a clear repository layer (TaskRepository, UserRepository, initialize_store) into a dedicated module, separating storage from route handlers and shrinking app.py by ~100 lines.
Preserves the existing atomic-write and lock discipline rather than weakening it, and keeps the migration semantics of init_db intact via initialize_store.

Removes duplicated inline store reads/writes across register, login, create_task, list/get/update_task, with no new duplication introduced (SonarQube duplications delta 0.0%) and no new bugs or smells.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound architectural refactor that extracts the flat-file persistence into a repository module with preserved atomicity and locking, carrying only minor per-request instantiation and lock-coupling nits alongside measured convention violations.

problems.description: flask_limiter is imported and wired in but no requirements.txt/pyproject change appears in the diff, so a fresh environment would fail on import/startup.

list_page_for_owner re-fetches the full sorted task list and linearly scans for the cursor on every page request (O(n) per call) — correct but not keyset pagination; acceptable for the flat-file store, but scales poorly if data grows.

Limiter is bound at import with a redis://localhost:6379/1 default storage URI, making app boot hard-depend on a reachable Redis (mitigated only by the conftest override for tests); a non-bootstrapping app is an availability coupling.

Mechanical convention score is 0.64, but several flagged violations live in untouched files (celery_config.py) and some appear to be module-level instance-name flags (e.g. the lowercase 'limiter' instance), not genuine misnames in the new code — a discrepancy versus the measurement worth noting.

strengths: Rate limiting on login with a user-scoped key and Retry-After header — a sound brute-force defense that follows the existing JWT/auth patterns.
Clean test seam: memory:// storage via conftest.py plus limiter.reset() per fixture, so tests need no external Redis.
Pagination is correctly validated (limit bounds, integer cursor), well-enveloped (data/next_cursor/total), and covered by dedicated tests.
Repository-layer implementation (list_page_for_owner) respects the existing repository/config-from-env/fixture conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested cross-cutting session (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects existing repository/config/test patterns, though it adds an un-manifested new dependency, an O(n)-per-page pagination path, and a Redis-boot coupling — with the 0.64 convention score partly inflated by pre-existing flags in untouched files.

compounding_issues: Global `_storage_lock` + full flat-file rewrite on every request (S1) never evolved: O(N) read-modify-write and fully serialized concurrency, which later features (auth lookups, notification owner resolution, pagination, rate-limit keying) all layered onto.
Hand-rolled HS256 JWT (S2) was never replaced with a vetted library (e.g. PyJWT) — a persistent security/verification burden through S5.
The owner_id migration (S2) backfills pre-auth tasks to owner_id=None, silently orphaning them with no claim path — old records become invisible to every user.
Cursor pagination (S5) is index-based over a list snapshot rather than keyset on (created_at, id), so tasks created between pages can be duplicated or skipped.
`_rate_limit_key()` (S5) performs a full store read under the lock on every request, compounding the flat-file performance ceiling with a per-request cross-cutting cost.
Repository hygiene: `__pycache__/*.pyc` bytecode and the `tasks.json` runtime state were committed to git in every session.
key_decisions: S1: Rebuilt the seed (SQLite/Blueprints/JWT) as a JSON flat-file store with atomic NamedTemporaryFile+replace writes and an app-wide Lock.
S1: Retained `init_db()` as the startup hook name to stay compatible with the framework's execution contract.
S2: Added hand-rolled HS256 JWT auth + werkzeug password hashing, gated all task endpoints behind `@jwt_required`, and scoped tasks per-owner via `owner_id` with an in-read migration.

S3: Introduced Celery/Redis async completion notifications with transition-edge detection (was_completed/became_completed) and graceful broker-outage fallback so a queue failure never breaks the task update.
S4: Extracted a Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) separating persistence from HTTP handlers — a genuine behavior-preserving refactor with zero test changes.
S5: Added cursor-based pagination (breaking /tasks response shape to {data, next_cursor, total}) and per-user/IP rate limiting via Flask-Limiter with memory:// for tests.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. S1 laid a clean, well-tested flat-file foundation with atomic writes and thread safety; S2 added authentication with explicit migration awareness for pre-existing stores; S3 added asynchronous integration (Celery notifications) with careful edge detection and fault tolerance; S4 was a genuine behavior-preserving architectural refactor into repositories; and S5 added cross-cutting hardening (pagination + rate limiting) that built directly on the S4 repository layer. The test suite grew in lockstep with the features, mocking external dependencies (Celery, Redis, rate-limit storage) rather than skipping coverage. The sole flat spot is structural: the flat-file store plus global lock was never revisited, so every subsequent layer inherited a serialized, O(N)-per-request persistence foundation.
